sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage B
sections.intro: Read “Ithaka” and answer questions 11–14. Mythological references are explained after the poem.

passage.title: Ithaka
passage.credit: —C.P. Cavafy · “Ithaka,” from C.P. Cavafy: Collected Poems (1992), translated by Edmund Keeley and Philip Sherrard, Princeton University Press

lines.text: As you set out for Ithaka
hope the voyage is a long one,
full of adventure, full of discovery.
Laistrygonians and Cyclops,²
angry Poseidon³—don’t be afraid of them:
you’ll never find things like that on your way
as long as you keep your thoughts raised high,
as long as a rare excitement
stirs your spirit and your body.
Laistrygonians and Cyclops,
wild Poseidon—you won’t encounter them
unless you bring them along inside your soul,
unless your soul sets them up in front of you.
Hope the voyage is a long one.
May there be many a summer morning when,
with what pleasure, what joy,
you come into harbors seen for the first time;
may you stop at Phoenician trading stations
to buy fine things,
mother of pearl and coral, amber and ebony,
sensual perfume of every kind—
as many sensual perfumes as you can;
and may you visit many Egyptian cities
to gather stores of knowledge from their scholars.
Keep Ithaka always in your mind.
Arriving there is what you are destined for.
But do not hurry the journey at all.
Better if it lasts for years,
so you are old by the time you reach the island,
wealthy with all you have gained on the way,
not expecting Ithaka to make you rich.
Ithaka gave you the marvelous journey.
Without her you would not have set out.
She has nothing left to give you now.
And if you find her poor, Ithaka won’t have fooled you.
Wise as you will have become, so full of experience,
you will have understood by then what these Ithakas mean.
¹ Ithaka — In the epic, The Odyssey, it took Odysseus 10 years to return to his Greek island home of Ithaka after winning the Trojan war
² Laistrygonians and Cyclops — monsters that Odysseus encountered on his journey home
³ Poseidon — the Greek god of the sea who sought to punish Odysseus for harming his son, a Cyclops

questions.prompt: The references to Laistrygonians, Cyclops, and Poseidon in the first stanza convey the idea that people
questions.explanation: The speaker says travelers will not encounter these threatening figures unless they carry them “inside [their] soul” and set them in their own way. This makes the obstacles partly self-created.

questions.prompt: The repetition in lines 2 and 14 stresses the
questions.explanation: Twice the speaker hopes for a long voyage. The many adventures, pleasures, and lessons along the way make the journey itself a metaphor for fully embracing life.

questions.prompt: As used in line 30, the concept of “wealthy” refers to
questions.explanation: The traveler gains knowledge and experience during the long voyage, while the poem says not to expect Ithaka itself to make one rich. “Wealthy” refers to accumulated insight, not money.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best clarifies what Ithaka represents?
questions.explanation: The poem says to keep Ithaka in mind because arriving there is “what you are destined for.” Ithaka represents the goal or destination that motivates the journey.
